# generator-shortcuts

The strongest plausible rival is **raw value equality**:

> For each aligned pair `(left[r,c], right[r,c])`, output `4` when the two raw
> color values are equal; otherwise output `0`.

This fits every canonical demonstration. Canonical left panels use foreground
`6`, right panels use foreground `5`, and both use background `0`. Thus raw
equality occurs exactly at `(0,0)`; an occupied pair is `(6,5)`, never equal.
The canonical examples therefore cannot distinguish equality from the intended
rule “both aligned cells are zero.”

A separating input emitted by the repaired generator is
`generate(0, 1, difficulty="medium", grid_h=3, left_color=6,
right_color=6, both_zero_count=1, layout="random")`:

```text
6 0 6 0 | 0 6 6 0
6 6 6 6 | 0 6 6 0
0 0 0 6 | 6 6 6 0
```

(The vertical bar only shows the boundary between adjacent 4-column panels; it
is not an input column.)

The intended output is:

```text
0 0 0 4
0 0 0 0
0 0 0 0
```

Raw-value equality instead produces:

```text
0 0 4 4
0 4 4 0
0 0 0 0
```

For example, row 1 / aligned column 3 is `(6,6)`: equality marks it `4`, while
the intended rule outputs `0` because neither cell is zero.

I checked this three ways:

1. `rule_mirror` produced the intended grid above;
2. the declared `raw_value_equality` rival produced the second grid;
3. the canonical Racket-backed semantic gate verified the named rival differs
   on generated same-color witnesses while matching all canonical pairs.

Yes, the proposed generator emits such cases systematically. Consecutive
sample indexes alternate different and same foreground colors, every ordinary
input contains a `11` pair, and `EXAMPLES_NEEDED = 2`. Therefore every
consecutive two-example lesson contains a same-color `11` counterexample to raw
value equality. The behavior is enforced by
`test_two_consecutive_examples_refute_raw_value_equality_shortcut` and declared
through `CANONICAL_SHORTCUTS`, `SEMANTIC_RIVALS`, and `WITNESS_RIVALS`.
